catalog_quote: [p.155] 2.3 STRESS The Anguthimri stress pattern is as follows: [p.156] (C)V́(C)CV(C)CV́(C)CV... i.e. the first syllable and every alternate syllable receives stress. The long-short distinction with vowels is only ever made in stressable syllables, and then only rarely in any syllable but the first. Thus, we find: /ðúʔu/ 'yamstick' /pá:na/ 'level' /kálipwa/ 'gully' /árana/ 'toenail, fingernail' /dʳé:gwati/ 'trevally' /bwáʔa/ 'meat' /ʔúnuwána/ 'blister' /máyuʔí:ni/ 'mullet' Note however that if an otherwise stressable syllable is the last of a word, it is not stressed. 2.4 MORPHOPHONEMICS ...

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at Crowley 1981:155-156 in the ANU scan we hold (text layer + 150 dpi page image with diacritics). (2) The classification rests on the only first-hand description of the language, a 49-page HAL grammar sketch with a dedicated stress section, by a professional descriptivist working with the last speaker; the language is dormant, so nothing better can appear. Coding 'fixed-strict, initial + alternating odd syllables L->R, no final stress' (stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10100 (1 = a stressed syllable)) matches Crowley's schema and all eight example forms exactly; the the primary-stress rule correctly notes Crowley does not rank primary vs secondary (the 'initial = main' reading is StressTyp2/Gordon's). (3) No list of works to obtain: Glottolog has no other grammar/phonology; secondary treatments (Hayes 1995:77, Gordon 2002, the StressTyp2 entry for this language) only restate Crowley. (4) The 'idn' flag (Mpakwathi vs Mpakwithi) is a StressTyp2 spelling vari
